title: Conejos County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Conejos County wells have a 100 ft median depth and 13.3 gpm median reported yield. Compare local records, water levels and finished-well costs.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Conejos County
intro_html:
A well budget in Conejos County starts with the parcel, not the county average. The median recorded depth is 100 feet, but the middle half runs from 50 to 184 feet—enough variation to change a drilling bid substantially.

Colorado DWR records include 5,676 permitted wells countywide, with 4,071 recorded as constructed. Use those records to narrow your search around La Jara, Sanford, Manassa, Romeo, Conejos, Antonito or Capulin, then check the completion records closest to the property.

sections.heading: A 100-Foot Median Is a Starting Point, Not a Target
sections.html:
Of the 4,088 wells reporting depth, the middle half reaches 50–184 feet. That is a useful bidding range, but not a promise that drilling can stop there. The 90th-percentile depth is 354 feet, and the deepest record reaches 4,000 feet; that extreme should not set a household budget.

Mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground makes the sequence of water-bearing layers important. Permits name Confined San Luis Valley and Confined San Luis Valley Aquifer, while many use an unnamed/fractured-bedrock category that does not establish parcel geology. Ask a driller to compare nearby logs, identify the likely producing interval and explain how extra depth or casing would affect the bid.

sections.heading: Reported Yields Are Encouraging, but Test the Actual Well
sections.html:
The 820 wells with reported pump yields have a 13.3 gpm median, with the middle half at 10.0–15.0 gpm. A household well performing in that range can be practical, provided a current pumping test confirms sustained production and recovery. A permit entry alone does not establish what an older well produces today.

Reported yields under 1 gpm account for 1%, while another 2% fall in the 1–5 gpm band. Low production is uncommon in this reporting subset, but it matters greatly to the affected buyer. Check storage needs, recovery and household demand before closing. Physical production also does not authorize irrigation or stock watering; the permit controls allowed uses.

sections.heading: Water at 25 Feet Does Not Mean a 25-Foot Well
sections.html:
Static water level is the resting depth to water inside a well, not its drilled depth. Among 384 reporting wells, the median is 25 feet below ground, and the middle half is 10–71 feet. In a confined aquifer, pressure can raise water above the layer where it enters the well.

Median measured levels were 30 feet in the 2000s, 17 feet in the 2010s and 30 feet in the 2020s. That series does not show a steady countywide decline. These are grouped records, not necessarily repeat measurements from the same wells. For a purchase, obtain current resting and pumping levels rather than treating the county series as a parcel forecast.

sections.heading: Conejos County's Permit History and Recorded Drillers
sections.html:
The permit history stretches from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2026. Issuance reached 1,009 in the 2000s, followed by 684 in the 2010s and 467 in the 2020s. The current decade is incomplete, and permit issuance is not the same as completed drilling.

The most active drillers in these records are Heersink Drilling (Heersink, Scott), with 416; Valley Pump Company (Self, Clinton L.), with 350; and Rocky Mountain Waterworks Llc (Phythian, Donald L.), with 224. Those counts show historical activity, not current availability or an endorsement. Domestic/household use appears on 73% of permits, but use categories overlap, so verify the actual authorization for any well you plan to buy.

sections.heading: Budget Beyond the Drilled Hole
sections.html:
For Conejos County's mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, the cost model uses $50–$75 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $5,000–$7,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $11,000–$19,500.

These are planning figures, not a parcel quote. The 50–184-foot middle depth range means a median-depth allowance can miss the actual scope. Ask for a written bid that separates drilling, casing, grout, well development and equipment. Confirm how access, trench routing and electrical service are handled, and how the contractor charges if the producing interval is deeper than expected.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality, Completion and Septic Layout
sections.html:
Environmental mapping identifies 2 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 14 historic mine features and 1 EPA Superfund/cleanup site within about 10 miles. Those map entries are reasons to investigate location and site status—not evidence that a particular household well is contaminated. The supplied records do not establish countywide drinking-water safety.

Have the actual well water tested, and ask the laboratory or local health authority whether nearby site history warrants additional sampling. Review casing, grout and wellhead condition for pathways that could admit surface contamination. A neighboring producing well does not guarantee success on an unbuilt parcel. Before fixing the house location, coordinate well placement, septic layout, drainage and drilling access.

sections.heading: Before Buying Near La Jara, Antonito or Capulin
sections.html:
Start with the permit tied to the property, then compare nearby constructed wells rather than every county permit. Around La Jara, Antonito or Capulin, look for completion logs with similar ground elevation, depth and named aquifer. Countywide medians are less useful than closely matched neighboring records.

For an existing home, request the completion report, recent pumping test, water-quality results and equipment history. For vacant land, confirm the proposed use with DWR before assuming a household well can supply livestock, landscaping or irrigation. Household-use permits can be restrictive, and augmentation requirements may apply. Make the purchase or building plan contingent on workable water authorization, drilling access and an approved septic layout.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Conejos County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth is 100 feet, and the middle half of wells runs from 50 to 184 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 354 feet. These figures come from 4,088 depth reports across the county. For a specific lot, nearby completion logs are a better guide than the county median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Conejos County?
faq.a: The planning model uses $50–$75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $5,000–$7,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $11,000–$19,500. Actual bids depend on depth, completion requirements, access and the equipment installation.

faq.q: How much water does a well produce in Conejos County?
faq.a: Among 820 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 13.3 gpm and the middle half is 10.0–15.0 gpm. Only 1% of reported yields are under 1 gpm, but that does not guarantee production on your parcel. Have an existing well tested for sustained pumping and recovery before relying on its recorded yield.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Conejos County?
faq.a: County permit records do not establish whether an individual well is safe to drink. Mapping shows 2 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 14 historic mine features and 1 EPA Superfund/cleanup site within about 10 miles. Proximity does not prove contamination. Test the actual well and use nearby environmental history to discuss additional sampling with a laboratory or health authority.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Conejos County?
faq.a: The available static-level series does not show a steady decline: median depths to water were 30 feet in the 2000s, 17 feet in the 2010s and 30 feet in the 2020s. Those groups may contain different wells. Obtain current measurements and any repeat measurements from the property rather than treating county medians as its trend.
